newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Housing Secretary Cisneros resigns post.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Housing Secretary Cisneros resigns post.

text.p: U.S. Housing Secretary Henry Cisneros submitted his resignation on Thursday, the latest Cabinet member to quit ahead of President Clinton's second term.
"I have concluded that I cannot ask to be considered for service in the next four years," Cisneros wrote in his resignation letter to Clinton.
Cisneros, 49, will stay as head of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) until Clinton's inauguration in January, a department spokesman said.
"The president thanks Secretary Cisneros for the outstanding work he's done at HUD and for being a good friend," Barry Toiv, a White House spokesman, said.
Cisneros had long been expected to leave his position and said earlier Thursday that a key deciding factor would be whether he could financially afford to stay on.
"I've been wrestling with this question about whether or not I could afford to stay," he told reporters hours before sending his resignation.

"I've got one daughter in law school ... who called me yesterday and asked me for some travel money that I'm not able to give her," he said. "It revolves basically around personal obligations. I just have to make a quick calculation of whether I think I can stretch this string any longer," Cisneros said.

Mayors of several major cities have been mentioned as potential successors, including Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell and Seattle Mayor Norm Rice. Another contender is Andrew Cuomo, assistant secretary at HUD and son of former New York Governor Mario Cuomo.
Cisneros, a former mayor himself, said he had informal discussions with Rice "about the attractiveness of him as a possible successor should I choose to not be considered."
He said he had also spoken with Campbell "basically exploring any possible areas of interest there might be."
Cisneros in 1981 became the first Hispanic mayor of a major U.S. city when he was elected Mayor of San Antonio, Texas.
Campbell was among a handful of big-city mayors who discussed urban issues with Vice President Al Gore at the White House on Thursday.
Asked whether he would take the position if offered, Campbell told reporters, "It is a decision that I would have to make with my family and with those who have been a part of my life in Atlanta."

Cisneros was dogged during his tenure at HUD by questions over payments he had made to a former mistress. He had made a public admission in the late 1980s that he had had an affair with onetime aide Linda Medlar.
An independent counsel was appointed to conduct an inquiry into whether Cisneros had lied to the FBI about the payments, and whether misstatements had an effect on his becoming a Cabinet member.
